claim: More than 6% of iMARGI-mapped read pairs had the RNA-end reads uniquely mapped to mtRNAs in each cell type profiled (H1, HFF, K562).
source: Surprisingly, in each cell type profiled, more than 6% of iMARGI-mapped read pairs had the RNA-end reads uniquely mapped to mtRNAs.
evidence: The manuscript reports a specific percentage of iMARGI reads mapping to mtRNAs based on experimental data from three cell types.

claim: 98.7% of mtRNA-matching sequences contain more than 5 bp mismatches to any NUMTs.
source: These large numbers of mtRNA reads cannot be due to errors mapping to the nuclear DNA of mitochondrial origin (NUMT) (Lopez et al., 1994), because 98.7% of mtRNA-matching sequences contain more than 5 bp mismatches to any NUMTs.
evidence: The manuscript provides a specific percentage based on sequence alignment analysis to exclude NUMT contamination.

claim: mtRNAs exhibited higher chromatin association level (CAL) than that of nuclear genome-transcribed RNAs (nuRNAs) in all three cell types (p = 0.0022, t-test).
source: Based on the normalized RNA-end reads, mtRNAs exhibited higher chromatin association level (CAL) than that of nuclear genome-transcribed RNAs (nuRNAs) in all three cell types (p = 0.0022, t-test) (Figure 1A).
evidence: The claim is supported by normalized iMARGI data with statistical testing and visualization in Figure 1A.

claim: mtRNAs show preferential attachment to promoter regions compared to other genomic regions in H1, HFF, and K562 cells.
source: iMARGI also revealed the attachment of mtRNAs to various genomic regions, including promoters, coding sequences (CDS), 5′ and 3′ untranslated regions (UTRs), enhancers, super enhancers (SEs), introns, and intergenic regions, with promoters showing the highest enrichment of mtRNA association in all three cell types (largest p = 0.0074, one-way analysis of variance [ANOVA]) (Figure 1B–D).
evidence: The manuscript reports iMARGI data showing enrichment at promoters with statistical significance and supporting figures.

claim: SncmtRNA showed higher CALs than that of nuRNA (p-value = 0.00017, Student's t-test).
source: SncmtRNA (GenBank: DQ386868.1), a mitochondria-encoded lncRNA that has been observed to be nuclear localized (Villegas et al., 2007; Burzio et al., 2009), is also one of the caRNAs and showed higher CALs than that of nuRNA (p-value = 0.00017, Student's t-test) (Figure 1A)
evidence: The claim is supported by iMARGI data with statistical testing and references to prior literature on SncmtRNA nuclear localization.

claim: SncmtRNA shows enriched association with promoters as compared to other genome regions.
source: SncmtRNA (GenBank: DQ386868.1), a mitochondria-encoded lncRNA that has been observed to be nuclear localized (Villegas et al., 2007; Burzio et al., 2009), is also one of the caRNAs and showed higher CALs than that of nuRNA (p-value = 0.00017, Student's t-test) (Figure 1A) and enriched association with promoters as compared to other genome regions (Figure 1E–G).
evidence: The claim is supported by iMARGI data showing genomic distribution patterns in Figures 1E-G.

claim: The CALs of mtRNA increased from NM to HT in human endothelial cells (p-value = 0.037, Student's t-test).
source: While ECs under NM control showed comparable levels of chromatin-attached mtRNAs as the other three cell types, the CALs of mtRNA increased from NM to HT (p-value = 0.037, Student's t-test) (Figure 1H).
evidence: The manuscript reports iMARGI data comparing two conditions with statistical testing.

claim: Read pairs between nuRNA and mitochondrial DNA (mtDNA) or mtRNA and mtDNA were barely detected under both NM and HT conditions.
source: In contrast, under both conditions, read pairs between nuRNA and mitochondrial DNA (mtDNA) or mtRNA and mtDNA were barely detected (Figure 1H), suggesting minimal mitochondrial contamination in the iMARGI libraries.
evidence: The manuscript reports iMARGI sequencing data as a control for mitochondrial contamination.

claim: The majority of mtRNAs exhibit higher levels of chromatin association than the nuRNAs under both NM and HT conditions in ECs.
source: Quantification of the CAL of mtRNAs, including coding and non-coding transcripts, indicated that the majority of mtRNAs exhibit not only abundant but also higher levels of chromatin association than the nuRNAs under both conditions in ECs (Figure 1I, J).
evidence: The claim is based on quantification of iMARGI data shown in Figures 1I and 1J.

claim: HT further induced the CALs of most of the mtRNAs compared to NM in ECs.
source: Moreover, comparison between NM and HT revealed that HT further induced the CALs of most of the mtRNAs (Figure 1K).
evidence: The manuscript reports comparative iMARGI data between two conditions shown in Figure 1K.

claim: SncmtRNA exhibited a 64-fold higher CAL than the average CAL of all nuRNAs in NM (p = 0.00082, Student's t-test).
source: Specifically, SncmtRNA exhibited a 64-fold higher CAL than the average CAL of all nuRNAs in NM (p = 0.00082, Student's t-test) (Figure 1I)
evidence: The manuscript reports a specific fold-change with statistical significance from iMARGI data.

claim: SncmtRNA CAL was further increased by HT compared to NM (p = 0.034, Student's t-test).
source: Specifically, SncmtRNA exhibited a 64-fold higher CAL than the average CAL of all nuRNAs in NM (p = 0.00082, Student's t-test) (Figure 1I), which was further increased by HT (p = 0.034, Student's t-test) (Figure 1K).
evidence: The manuscript reports comparative iMARGI data with statistical testing.

claim: 312 HT-induced genes were identified in ECs from RNA-seq (adjusted p-value <0.05).
source: To this end, we identified 312 HT-induced genes in ECs from RNA-seq (adjusted p-value <0.05).
evidence: The manuscript reports RNA-seq analysis results with a specific statistical threshold.

claim: The promoters of HT-induced genes exhibited higher CAL of mtRNAs compared to other gene promoters and other genomic regions (p = 0.029, Student's t-test).
source: Compared with other gene promoters, and other genomic regions including enhancers, SEs, introns, 5′ and 3′ UTRs, CDS, and intergenic regions, the promoters of HT-induced genes exhibited higher CAL of mtRNAs (p = 0.029, Student's t-test) (Figure 1L, M)
evidence: The claim is supported by iMARGI data analysis with statistical testing shown in Figures 1L and 1M.

claim: The promoters of HT-induced genes exhibited higher CAL of SncmtRNA compared to other genomic regions (p = 0.016, Student's t-test).
source: Compared with other gene promoters, and other genomic regions including enhancers, SEs, introns, 5′ and 3′ UTRs, CDS, and intergenic regions, the promoters of HT-induced genes exhibited higher CAL of mtRNAs (p = 0.029, Student's t-test) (Figure 1L, M) and SncmtRNA (p = 0.016, Student's t-test) (Figure 1N, O).
evidence: The claim is supported by iMARGI data analysis with statistical testing shown in Figures 1N and 1O.

claim: SncmtRNA is comprised of 1559 nt sequence encoding mitochondrial 16S rRNA (transcribed from the H strand of mitochondrial genome), with its 5′ end appended to an 815 nt invert repeat, forming a putative double-stranded hairpin-shaped structure.
source: As described (Villegas et al., 2007; Burzio et al., 2009), SncmtRNA is comprised of 1559 nt sequence encoding mitochondrial 16S rRNA (transcribed from the H strand of mitochondrial genome), with its 5′ end appended to an 815 nt invert repeat, forming a putative double-stranded hairpin-shaped structure (Figure 2A, Figure 2—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: The claim is based on prior literature describing SncmtRNA structure and confirmed by the authors' analysis.

claim: The presence of SncmtRNA in ECs was verified using RT-PCR with primers flanking the putative hairpin loop and the unique junction region, followed by Sanger sequencing.
source: Based on this description, we verified the presence of SncmtRNA in ECs using reverse transcription (RT)-polymerase chain reaction (PCR) with primers flanking the putative hairpin loop and the unique junction region (Figure 2A, B), followed by Sanger sequencing (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: The manuscript describes experimental validation using RT-PCR and sequencing.

claim: PCR without RT failed to amplify SncmtRNA, indicating it is an RNA.
source: As a control, PCR without RT failed to amplify SncmtRNA, evident of an RNA.
evidence: The manuscript reports a negative control experiment confirming RNA nature of the molecule.

claim: In Rho0 cells that are depleted of mtDNA, SncmtRNA, like 16S rRNA, was not detected.
source: Moreover, in Rho0 cells that are depleted of mtDNA (Chandel and Schumacker, 1999), SncmtRNA, like 16S rRNA, was not detected (Figure 2B), indicative of its mitochondrial origin.
evidence: The manuscript reports experimental data from Rho0 cells confirming mitochondrial origin.

claim: FISH detected abundant SncmtRNA signals in the nucleus of ECs.
source: We also performed fluorescence in situ hybridization (FISH) with an antisense locked nucleic acid (LNA) probe targeting the unique junction region of SncmtRNA, which detected abundant signals in the nucleus in ECs.
evidence: The manuscript reports FISH imaging data showing nuclear localization.

claim: FISH detected SncmtRNA signals in the cytoplasm resembling the morphology of mitochondria.
source: FISH also detected SncmtRNA signals in the cytoplasm resembling the morphology of mitochondria (Figure 2C).
evidence: The manuscript reports FISH imaging data showing cytoplasmic/mitochondrial localization.

claim: The majority of SncmtRNA is localized in the nuclear fractions including chromatin and nucleoplasm.
source: Consistently, qPCR of SncmtRNA in different EC subcellular fractions detected the majority of SncmtRNA in the nuclear fractions including chromatin and nucleoplasm, with MALAT1 (predominantly nuclear localized), GAPDH (predominantly cytoplasm localized), and TUG1 (localized in both nucleus and cytoplasm) quantified as controls (Figure 2D).
evidence: The manuscript reports qPCR data from subcellular fractionation experiments.

claim: HT increased chromatin-associated SncmtRNA in ECs, while there was no change for MALAT1, TUG1, and GAPDH.
source: Moreover, compared to NM, HT-increased chromatin-associated SncmtRNA in ECs, while there was no change for MALAT1, TUG1, and GAPDH (Figure 2D).
evidence: The manuscript reports comparative qPCR data from subcellular fractions under two conditions.

claim: High glucose and TNFα are known to impair mitochondrial biogenesis.
source: Arguing against this possibility, high glucose and TNFα are known to impair mitochondrial biogenesis (Shenouda et al., 2011; Trudeau et al., 2010).
evidence: The claim is based on cited literature about the effects of high glucose and TNFα.

claim: Several nuclear-encoded genes regulating mitochondrial biogenesis, such as PPARG and TFAM, were downregulated by HT in ECs.
source: Consistently, bulk RNA-seq of ECs under NM vs HT revealed that several nuclear-encoded genes regulating mitochondrial biogenesis, such as peroxisome proliferator-activated recepter gamma (PPARG) and Transcription Factor A, Mitochondrial (TFAM) were downregulated (Figure 2—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: The manuscript reports RNA-seq data showing gene expression changes.

claim: Mitochondria visualized by Mitotracker showed fragmentation under HT.
source: Additionally, mitochondria visualized by Mitotracker showed fragmentation under HT (Figure 2—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: The manuscript reports imaging data showing mitochondrial morphology changes.

claim: The majority of mitochondria-encoded transcripts remained unchanged between NM and HT.
source: In terms of mitochondria-encoded transcripts, the majority remained unchanged (Figure 2—figure supplement 1F).
evidence: The manuscript reports RNA-seq data comparing mitochondrial transcript levels.

claim: The total RNA levels of SncmtRNA as well as 16S rRNA and ASncmtRNA were comparable between NM and HT.
source: Similarly, the total RNA levels of SncmtRNA as well as 16S rRNA and antisense mitochondrial non-coding RNA (ASncmtRNA), all derived from MT-RNR2, were comparable between NM and HT.
evidence: The manuscript reports qPCR data comparing total RNA levels between conditions.

claim: The expression of eNOS was decreased by HT in ECs.
source: In contrast, the expression of endothelial nitric oxide synthase (eNOS), hallmark of EC homeostasis was decreased, and that of VCAM1 and ICAM1, typical inflammation markers were strongly induced by HT (Figure 2E).
evidence: The manuscript reports qPCR data showing gene expression changes in response to HT.

claim: VCAM1 and ICAM1 were strongly induced by HT in ECs.
source: In contrast, the expression of endothelial nitric oxide synthase (eNOS), hallmark of EC homeostasis was decreased, and that of VCAM1 and ICAM1, typical inflammation markers were strongly induced by HT (Figure 2E).
evidence: The manuscript reports qPCR data showing gene expression changes in response to HT.

claim: LNA-S1 (LNA-S) consistently decreased SncmtRNA level without affecting those of 16S rRNA and ASncmtRNAs.
source: As expected, only LNA-S1 (hereafter termed LNA-S) consistently decreased SncmtRNA level without affecting those of 16S rRNA and ASncmtRNAs (Figure 2—figure supplement 2B) and was thus used in the subsequent SncmtRNA knockdown (Snc-KD) experiments.
evidence: The manuscript reports qPCR data showing selective knockdown of SncmtRNA.

claim: LNA-S decreased the total cellular SncmtRNA in ECs under both NM and HT.
source: While LNA-S decreased the total cellular SncmtRNA in ECs under both NM and HT (Figure 2F)
evidence: The manuscript reports qPCR data showing knockdown efficiency.

claim: The inhibitory effect of LNA-S on SncmtRNA was primarily in the nucleus.
source: While LNA-S decreased the total cellular SncmtRNA in ECs under both NM and HT (Figure 2F), the inhibitory effect was primarily in the nucleus (Figure 2G).
evidence: The manuscript reports qPCR data from subcellular fractionation showing nuclear-specific effect.

claim: Under NM, Snc-KD resulted in 265 differentially expressed genes (DEGs), including 160 down- and 105-upregulated.
source: Bulk RNA-seq revealed that under NM, Snc-KD resulted in 265 differentially expressed genes (DEGs), including 160 down- and 105-upregulated (Figure 2—figure supplement 2C).
evidence: The manuscript reports RNA-seq analysis results.

claim: Under HT, Snc-KD led to 732 DEGs (403 down- and 329 upregulated) in ECs.
source: Under HT, Snc-KD led to more DEGs, that is 732 DEGs (403 down- and 329 upregulated) in ECs (Figure 2—figure supplement 2D)
evidence: The manuscript reports RNA-seq analysis results.

claim: There were 120 common DEGs between NM and HT upon Snc-KD.
source: Under HT, Snc-KD led to more DEGs, that is 732 DEGs (403 down- and 329 upregulated) in ECs (Figure 2—figure supplement 2D), with 120 common DEGs between NM and HT (Figure 2—figure supplement 2E).
evidence: The manuscript reports comparative RNA-seq analysis results.

claim: Innate immune and inflammatory responses are the most consistently affected pathways by Snc-KD under both NM and HT.
source: Pathway enrichment analysis indicated that innate immune and inflammatory responses are the most consistently affected pathways under both NM and HT, with more pathways involved in innate immune response under NM (e.g. Type I interferon signaling and cellular response to virus and LPS) and more pathways involved in inflammatory response under HT (e.g., TNF signaling, leukocyte migration, and cell–cell adhesion) (Figure 2H, I).
evidence: The manuscript reports pathway enrichment analysis of RNA-seq data.

claim: Hallmark genes for innate immune and inflammatory activation, including DDX58, MX2, VCAM1, and ICAM1, were strongly suppressed by Snc-KD under both NM and HT.
source: For example, hallmark genes for innate immune and inflammatory activation, including DDX58, MX2, VCAM1, and ICAM1, were strongly suppressed by Snc-KD under both NM and HT (Figure 2J).
evidence: The manuscript reports RNA-seq data showing specific gene expression changes.

claim: The HT-induced pro-inflammatory response of ECs assayed by monocyte adhesion was abrogated by Snc-KD.
source: Consistent with the gene expression changes, the HT-induced pro-inflammatory response of ECs assayed by monocyte adhesion, was abrogated by Snc-KD (Figure 2K and L).
evidence: The manuscript reports functional assay data showing effect on monocyte adhesion.

claim: Cell proliferation, cell division, and cell cycle regulation were mostly upregulated by Snc-KD, especially under HT.
source: In contrast, cell proliferation, cell division, and cell cycle regulation were mostly upregulated by Snc-KD, especially under HT (Figure 2I, Figure 2—figure supplement 2H)
evidence: The manuscript reports pathway enrichment analysis of RNA-seq data.

claim: Cell cycle regulators CDK1 and CCNB1 were significantly induced by Snc-KD.
source: In contrast, cell proliferation, cell division, and cell cycle regulation were mostly upregulated by Snc-KD, especially under HT (Figure 2I, Figure 2—figure supplement 2H), evident by the significant induction of cell cycle regulators, for example, CDK1 and CCNB1 (Figure 2M).
evidence: The manuscript reports RNA-seq data showing specific gene expression changes.

claim: HT caused a cell cycle arrest at G1 phase, while LNA-S led to a trend toward promoting the G1-arrested cells to S phase.
source: Fluorescence ubiquitination cell cycle indicator (FUCCI) assay, which detects cell cycle progression and division (Sakaue-Sawano et al., 2008), revealed while HT caused a cell cycle arrest at G1 phase, LNA-S led to a trend toward promoting the G1-arrested cells to S phase (Figure 2N, O).
evidence: The manuscript reports FUCCI assay data showing cell cycle distribution changes.

claim: Snc-KD had no clear effect on mitochondria network or morphology.
source: In contrast, Snc-KD had no clear effect on mitochondria network or morphology (Figure 2—figure supplement 3A–F).
evidence: The manuscript reports imaging data showing no effect on mitochondrial structure.

claim: Snc-KD led to minimal changes in mitochondrial function as quantified by oxygen consumption rate (OCR) using Seahorse assay.
source: Furthermore, Snc-KD led to minimal changes in mitochondrial function as quantified by oxygen consumption rate (OCR) using Seahorse assay (Figure 2—figure supplement 3G).
evidence: The manuscript reports Seahorse assay data showing no significant effect on mitochondrial respiration.

claim: Snc-KD did not cause any significant effect on the levels of mtRNAs or those of nuclear-encoded genes regulating mitochondrial biogenesis.
source: Additionally, we did not observe any significant effect on the levels of mtRNAs or those of nuclear-encoded genes regulating mitochondrial biogenesis upon Snc-KD (Figure 2—figure supplement 3H–K).
evidence: The manuscript reports RNA-seq data showing no effect on mitochondrial gene expression.

claim: 14 HT-induced genes exhibit significant increase in the promoter-associated SncmtRNA (Benjamini–Hochberg adjusted p-value <0.05).
source: Based on the iMARGI and RNA-seq data from ECs under NM vs HT, we identified 14 HT-induced genes that exhibit significant increase in the promoter-associated SncmtRNA (Benjamini–Hochberg adjusted p-value <0.05) (Figure 2—figure supplement 4A).
evidence: The manuscript reports integrated analysis of iMARGI and RNA-seq data.

claim: Out of 14 genes with increased SncmtRNA-promoter association, Snc-KD reduced the expression levels of 12 of them under HT, including 6 with statistical significance (ICAM1, ZFHX2, ABCA6, CSF1, PDE5A, and RND1).
source: Out of these 14 genes, Snc-KD reduced the expression levels of 12 of them under HT (Snc-KD vs Scr fold-change <1), including 6 (ICAM1, ZFHX2, ABCA6, CSF1, PDE5A, and RND1) with statistical significance (Benjamini–Hochberg adjusted p-value <0.05), suggesting the genes suppressed by Snc-KD are enriched in these genes (odds ratio = 2.82, p-value = 0.0096, Chi-square test) (Figure 2—figure supplement 4B).
evidence: The manuscript reports RNA-seq data with statistical analysis showing enrichment.

claim: snRNA-seq and scRNA-seq were highly correlated (Spearman correlation coefficient [SCC] = 0.9).
source: While snRNA- and scRNA-seq were highly correlated (Spearman correlation coefficient [SCC] = 0.9) (Figure 3A–C and Figure 3—figure supplement 1C, D)
evidence: The manuscript reports correlation analysis between two sequencing methods.

claim: snRNA-seq identified 462 DEGs (comprising 302 down- and 160 upregulated) upon Snc-KD in HT.
source: While snRNA- and scRNA-seq were highly correlated (Spearman correlation coefficient [SCC] = 0.9) (Figure 3A–C and Figure 3—figure supplement 1C, D), snRNA-seq identified 462 DEGs (comprising 302 down- and 160 upregulated)
evidence: The manuscript reports snRNA-seq analysis results.

claim: scRNA-seq returned 318 DEGs (comprising 174 down- and 144 upregulated) upon Snc-KD in HT.
source: While snRNA- and scRNA-seq were highly correlated (Spearman correlation coefficient [SCC] = 0.9) (Figure 3A–C and Figure 3—figure supplement 1C, D), snRNA-seq identified 462 DEGs (comprising 302 down- and 160 upregulated) and scRNA-seq returned 318 DEGs (comprising 174 down- and 144 upregulated) as a result of Snc-KD in HT (Figure 3—figure supplement 1E, F).
evidence: The manuscript reports scRNA-seq analysis results.

claim: Among common DEGs shared by sc- and snRNA-seq, 100 were downregulated and 33 were upregulated by Snc-KD.
source: Among common DEGs shared by sc- and snRNA-seq, 100 were downregulated and 33 were upregulated by Snc-KD, suggesting that SncmtRNA is more likely to be a transcriptional activator than suppressor (Figure 3F).
evidence: The manuscript reports comparative analysis of sc- and snRNA-seq data.

claim: 43 genes were consistently downregulated in bulk RNA-seq and sn- and scRNA-seq by Snc-KD, including ICAM1, VCAM1, CCL2, and DDX58.
source: Among these common DEGs, 43 were consistently downregulated in bulk RNA-seq and sn- and scRNA-seq, including ICAM1, VCAM1, CCL2, and DDX58 (Figure 3G, Figure 3—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: The manuscript reports integrated analysis of multiple RNA-seq datasets.

claim: The 43 consistently downregulated genes showed higher correlation between snRNA and scRNA-seq (SCC = 0.65) as compared to other DEGs (SCC = 0.26).
source: The 43 consistently downregulated genes showed higher correlation between snRNA and scRNA-seq (SCC = 0.65) as compared to other DEGs (SCC = 0.26) (Figure 3H, I), suggesting that these genes are more likely to be regulated at the transcriptional level by SncmtRNA.
evidence: The manuscript reports correlation analysis suggesting transcriptional regulation mechanism.

claim: Snc-KD led to a reduction of nascent transcripts of ICAM1 and VCAM1 in ECs exposed to HT.
source: To test our hypothesis, we performed nascent RNA pull-down assay to demonstrate that Snc-KD indeed led to a reduction of nascent transcripts of ICAM1 and VCAM1 in ECs exposed to HT (Figure 3J).
evidence: The manuscript reports nascent RNA pull-down assay data.

claim: SncmtRNA overexpression (Snc-OE) strongly induced ICAM1 and VCAM1, but not that of eNOS and KLF2.
source: Complementarily, we overexpressed SncmtRNA (Snc-OE) in ECs using AAV9, which enters the nucleus and drives the transcription of SncmtRNA (Wang et al., 2019). Snc-OE strongly induced ICAM1 and VCAM1, but not that of eNOS and KLF2 (Figure 3K).
evidence: The manuscript reports qPCR data from overexpression experiments with citation for the AAV9 method.

claim: Snc-OE resulted in 553 DEGs (289 down- and 264 upregulated).
source: At a transcriptome level, Snc-OE resulted in 553 DEGs (289 down- and 264 upregulated), among which similar pathways to those affected by Snc-KD, for example Type I interferon signaling and responses to virus and lipopolysaccharide were also enriched (Figure 3L).
evidence: The manuscript reports RNA-seq analysis results from overexpression experiments.

claim: Snc-OE in HEK-293 cells increased the luciferase activity driven by promoters containing binding elements of IRF3/7.
source: Consistently, Snc-OE in HEK-293 cells also increased the luciferase activity driven by promoters containing binding elements of IRF3/7, key TF mediating Type-I IFN signaling (Figure 3M).
evidence: The manuscript reports luciferase reporter assay data.

claim: MT-CYB and MT-ND5 showed high CAL that was further increased by HT in ECs.
source: Specifically, we performed single-molecule RNA FISH (smFISH) in ECs for MT-CYB and MT-ND5, which showed high CAL (Figure 1I–K) that was further increased by HT in ECs and have sequences feasible for smFISH probe design.
evidence: The manuscript reports iMARGI data showing chromatin association levels.

claim: smFISH for MT-CYB and MT-ND5 detected signals largely overlapping with that of Mitotracker.
source: While the positive control (POLR2A, a universally expressed gene) detected strong punctate signals and the negative control (dapB, a bacterial gene not expressed in humans) yielded no specific signals (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A, B), smFISH for MT-CYB and MT-ND5 detected signals largely overlapping with that of Mitotracker (Figure 4—figure supplement 1C, D).
evidence: The manuscript reports smFISH imaging data showing mitochondrial localization.

claim: smFISH with Rho0 cells showed no signals of either MT-CYB or MT-ND5, indicating that the probes indeed detected mitochondrial transcripts.
source: In contrast, smFISH with Rho0 cells showed no signals of either of the mtRNAs, indicating that the probes indeed detected mitochondrial transcripts (Figure 4—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: The manuscript reports negative control smFISH data confirming specificity.

claim: Confocal microscopy revealed a fraction of MT-CYB and MT-ND5 signals in the nuclei as clear puncta, which overlapped with that of DAPI in ECs under NM and significantly increased by HT.
source: At higher magnification, confocal microscopy revealed a fraction of MT-CYB and MT-ND5 signals in the nuclei as clear puncta, which overlapped with that of DAPI in ECs under NM and significantly increased by HT (Figure 4A–C).
evidence: The manuscript reports confocal microscopy imaging data showing nuclear localization.

claim: A fraction of MT-CYB signals overlapped those of SC35 in HT-treated ECs.
source: As shown in Figure 4H, I, in HT-treated ECs, a fraction of MT-CYB signals overlapped those of SC35, and the signals of MT-CYB showed proximity to those of HT-induced VCAM1 and LINC00607 pre-mRNAs.
evidence: The manuscript reports co-immunofluorescence and smFISH imaging data.

claim: The signals of MT-CYB showed proximity to those of HT-induced VCAM1 and LINC00607 pre-mRNAs in HT-treated ECs.
source: As shown in Figure 4H, I, in HT-treated ECs, a fraction of MT-CYB signals overlapped those of SC35, and the signals of MT-CYB showed proximity to those of HT-induced VCAM1 and LINC00607 pre-mRNAs.
evidence: The manuscript reports sequential smFISH imaging data showing spatial proximity.

claim: smFISH detected nuclear MT-CYB signals in ECs from all four human donors (two non-diabetic and two T2D).
source: In agreement with data from cultured ECs, smFISH detected nuclear MT-CYB signals in ECs from all four donors.
evidence: The manuscript reports smFISH imaging data from human donor samples.

claim: T2D donor-derived ECs exhibited more nuclear localized MT-CYB puncta compared to non-diabetic donors.
source: Furthermore, T2D donor-derived ECs exhibited more nuclear localized MT-CYB puncta compared to non-diabetic donors (Figure 5B, C).
evidence: The manuscript reports quantitative smFISH imaging data from human donor samples.

claim: Mitochondria possess their own circular and double-stranded genome (mtDNA) of 16.5 kb in size.
source: As derivatives of endosymbiotic bacterial ancestors, mitochondria in eukaryotes possess their own circular and double-stranded genome (mtDNA) of 16.5 kb in size.
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about mitochondrial genome structure.

claim: mtDNA is bidirectionally transcribed to produce 13 mRNAs, 2 rRNAs, and 22 tRNAs involved in oxidative phosphorylation (OXPHOS).
source: mtDNA is bidirectionally transcribed to produce 13 mRNAs, 2 rRNAs, and 22 tRNAs involved in oxidative phosphorylation (OXPHOS).
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about mitochondrial transcription products.

claim: The mitochondrial genome also produces non-coding RNAs (ncRNAs) including small RNAs and long ncRNAs (lncRNAs), whose functions are yet to be fully characterized.
source: The mitochondrial genome also produces non-coding RNAs (ncRNAs) including small RNAs and long ncRNAs (lncRNAs), whose functions are yet to be fully characterized (Mercer et al., 2011; Rackham et al., 2011; Ro et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is based on cited literature about mitochondrial ncRNAs.

claim: Nucleus-encoded transcription factors such as NRF1 and TFAM regulate mitochondrial biogenesis, mtDNA replication, and transcription.
source: For example, nucleus-encoded transcription factors (TFs) such as NRF1 and TFAM, co-regulators such as PGC1α, and the RNA polymerase POLRMT regulate mitochondrial biogenesis, mtDNA replication, and transcription (Gleyzer et al., 2005; Virbasius and Scarpulla, 1994; Ojala et al., 1981; Falkenberg et al., 2002; Kühl et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is based on multiple cited studies about nuclear control of mitochondrial function.

claim: Nucleus-transcribed non-coding RNAs (ncRNAs) have been shown to regulate mitochondrial RNA (mtRNA) processing and translation.
source: Nucleus-transcribed non-coding RNAs (ncRNAs) have also been shown to regulate mitochondrial RNA (mtRNA) processing and translation (Vendramin et al., 2018; Puranam and Attardi, 2001; Zhang et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is based on cited literature about nuclear ncRNA regulation of mitochondria.

claim: Mitochondria can communicate with nucleus through mitochondrial retrograde signaling, typically mediated by reactive oxygen species, ATP, and Ca2+.
source: Conversely, mitochondria can communicate with nucleus through mitochondrial retrograde signaling, typically mediated by reactive oxygen species, ATP, and Ca2+ (De Stefani et al., 2016; Liu and Butow, 2006; Vizioli et al., 2020).
evidence: The claim is based on cited literature about mitochondrial retrograde signaling mechanisms.

claim: Mitochondria-derived short peptides have been shown to regulate nuclear gene expression.
source: Mitochondria-derived short peptides have also been shown to regulate nuclear gene expression (Reynolds et al., 2021).
evidence: The claim is based on cited literature about mitochondrial peptides.

claim: Mitochondria DNA (mtDNA) and double-stranded RNAs (dsRNAs) can be released into the cytoplasm, which turn on an endogenous 'danger signal' to trigger a type-I interferon response and innate immune surveillance.
source: Moreover, mitochondria DNA (mtDNA) and double-stranded RNAs (dsRNAs) can also be released into the cytoplasm, which turn on an endogenous 'danger signal' to trigger a type-I interferon response and innate immune surveillance (Huang et al., 2020; Maekawa et al., 2019; West et al., 2015; Dhir et al., 2018; Tigano et al., 2021).
evidence: The claim is based on multiple cited studies about mitochondrial danger signaling.

claim: MT-RNR2-derived sense non-coding mitochondrial RNA (SncmtRNA) has been detected in the nucleus of human endothelial cells (ECs) and several cancer cell lines.
source: Burzio et al. detected MT-RNR2-derived sense non-coding mitochondrial RNA (SncmtRNA) in the nucleus of human endothelial cells (ECs) and several cancer cell lines (Villegas et al., 2007; Burzio et al., 2009; Landerer et al., 2011).
evidence: The claim is based on cited literature about SncmtRNA nuclear localization.

claim: A small mitochondrial-encoded ncRNA, mito-ncR-805, has been identified as localized in the nucleus of alveolar epithelial cells, and correlated with the increased expression of nuclear-encoded genes that regulate mitochondrial function.
source: Perry et al. identified a small mitochondrial-encoded ncRNA, mito-ncR-805, localized in the nucleus of alveolar epithelial cells, and correlated with the increased expression of nuclear-encoded genes that regulate mitochondrial function (Blumental-Perry et al., 2020).
evidence: The claim is based on cited literature about another nuclear-localized mtRNA.

claim: Chromatin-associated RNAs (caRNAs) form a critical layer of the epigenome that can regulate nuclear transcription.
source: The chromatin-associated RNAs (caRNAs) form a critical layer of the epigenome that can regulate nuclear transcription (Li and Fu, 2019; Nguyen et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim is based on cited literature about caRNAs and their regulatory role.

claim: Snc-KD also attenuated LPS-induced inflammatory gene expression, including DDX58, VCAM1, and ICAM1.
source: Indeed, Snc-KD also attenuated LPS-induced inflammatory gene expression, including DDX58, VCAM1, and ICAM1 (Figure 2—figure supplement 5).
evidence: The manuscript reports qPCR data from LPS stimulation experiments.
